name: Kimono
blurb: T-shaped Japanese robe wrapped left over right and tied with an obi; kimono vs yukata
title: Kimono vs Yukata: Wrapping, Obi & Drawing Reference
description: Kimono reference: kimono vs yukata, the left-over-right rule, obi and furisode, how to draw the sleeves and folds, and posing tips for kimono photos.
answer: The kimono is the traditional Japanese robe: a T-shaped, straight-seamed garment with wide sleeves, wrapped around the body left side over right and held with a wide sash called an obi. The yukata is its light, unlined cotton cousin, worn casually in summer and at festivals.

sections.h: Kimono basics and the left-over-right rule
body: A kimono is cut from straight panels of fabric, so its shape comes from how it is wrapped and tied, not from tailoring. The wearer's left panel always goes over the right. Wrapping it right over left is reserved for dressing the deceased, so getting the direction wrong is a noticeable mistake in drawings and photos.
Kimono are now mostly worn for ceremonies such as weddings, coming-of-age day, tea ceremony and New Year, while yukata are popular at summer festivals and fireworks displays.

body: A formal kimono outfit adds an under-kimono collar showing at the neck, obi accessories such as the obijime cord, tabi socks and zori sandals.

ul: Draw the collar as a V that closes left over right and sits a little away from the back of the neck; the back collar dips to show the nape.
The body is a fairly straight tube from chest to ankles. Kimono flatten curves, so avoid tight waist shaping.
The obi is a wide band around the waist; most of the decoration is the knot at the back, so plan a back or three-quarter view to show it.
Sleeves hang from the arm in a rectangle with a rounded lower corner; the long sleeves of a furisode almost reach the ankles.
Steps are short because the skirt is narrow; the hem wraps tightly around the ankles.

body: If you are not used to dressing in kimono, a yukata is much easier to put on yourself. Check the wrap direction in a mirror and keep the collar crossing neatly at the throat.

Kimono reward quiet, graceful posture: knees together, small steps, one hand holding the opposite sleeve when reaching out. Looking back over the shoulder shows both the nape and the obi knot. Gardens, wooden houses, shrines (where photography is allowed) and festival lanterns are classic settings.

faq.q: Which side goes on top in a kimono?
faq.a: The wearer's left side goes over the right. Right over left is used only when dressing the deceased.

faq.q: What is the difference between a kimono and a yukata?
faq.a: A yukata is a lightweight, unlined cotton robe for summer and casual events. A kimono is usually silk, lined and worn with more layers and accessories.
The obi is the wide sash wrapped around the waist of a kimono or yukata and tied in a decorative knot, usually at the back.
